meta.regime: The two shocks that have run against each other on this board all autumn have both now turned, and in the same direction. The Middle East energy premium, the inflationary one, broke hard: Brent settled 8.7% lower on Wednesday and is minus 15.07% on the week at 94.106, WTI is 87.186 and minus 14.52%, and the entire gas complex followed with EU gas minus 13.01% and German gas minus 12.17%. The AI capital-spending repricing, the disinflationary one, had its monetary leg reverse on the midterm result while its demand leg stayed broken - gold is 4112.65 and plus 1.29% on falling real yields, copper is 6.3621 and minus 3.33% on the week. The consequence is that six of these eight central banks built hawkish cases on an energy input that has just fallen 12% to 15% in five sessions.

US and Canadian employment then print together Friday at 13:30Z, Ueda speaks Friday 16:00Z and New Zealand votes Saturday.

dailyRead: The thing that changed overnight is bigger than any single data point, and it runs underneath seven of the eight currencies here. Brent settled 8.98 dollars lower on Wednesday, down 8.7% to 94.62, and WTI fell 7.97 dollars or 8.3% to 88.12 - the largest single-session break of the entire Hormuz regime. TradingEconomics now has Brent at 94.106 and minus 15.07% on the week, WTI at 87.186 and minus 14.52%, gasoline minus 12.38%, heating oil minus 9.43%. The gas complex went with it: EU gas 85.18 and minus 13.01% on the week, German gas 89.58 and minus 12.17%, UK gas minus 12.50%. Now hold that against what this board actually owns. The Bank of England hikes to 4.00% in six hours because energy pushed UK CPI to 3.5%. The euro area printed a 4.0% October HICP yesterday because energy inflation jumped to 20.8% from 18.9%. Switzerland's 1.5% CPI surprise was roughly 96% energy. Macklem told the Commons finance committee on November 3 that Canada's inflation pickup came from the Middle East energy shock rather than domestic demand. The RBA built its November 3 hike on elevated fuel and commodity prices. Every one of those cases was measured on prices that have now fallen 12% to 15% in five sessions. The hikes themselves still happen - they are dated and priced - but the forward paths beyond the next meeting are where the mispricing now sits, and the risk is to the dovish side everywhere except the United States. That is the trade this file is making today. Second, the part that is not a de-escalation story, which matters because the market is treating it as one. Crude fell on three things: Trump saying there are no immediate plans to strike Iran, the Democratic sweep being read as constraining his military options, and Middle Eastern oil exports recovering to roughly pre-war levels. But the Strait itself has not reopened and the diplomacy went backwards on the same day. Iran rejected Washington's response to its conditions for reopening Hormuz on November 4, Iran has sharply increased attacks on shipping, and only seven commodity vessels transited the Strait on Thursday against seventeen a day earlier. Treasury Secretary Bessent describing vessel movement as increasing day by day is contested by those counts. So crude is now priced for a resolution that Tehran has formally refused, which makes the risk asymmetric to the upside from here and is why USOIL is a RANGE rather than a short after a 15% week. Third, the dollar, where the verdict and the forward genuinely disagree. Democrats took both chambers - the sweep is confirmed now rather than probable, the Dow jumped 1,569 points or about 3%, the ten-year fell 8.8 basis points to 4.886% and the two-year to 4.58%. DXY is 101.250, minus 0.24% today and minus 0.77% on the week, a one-month low. But October ADP private payrolls came in at plus 86,000 against a forecast near 75,000, and December hike pricing rebuilt to roughly 76% to 82% across trackers from the 71% to 73% this file carried yesterday. The United States is the only economy on this board whose hike case never depended on energy: CPI 3.7%, core 2.6%, PPI 6.3%. So the dollar fell for fiscal reasons that are now fully resolved and in the price, while its rate case firmed. Friday's payrolls at a plus 65,000 forecast is where that contradiction breaks. Fourth, the metals, which split the same way they did yesterday but harder. Gold is 4112.65 and plus 1.29%, plus 2.27% on the week, through 4100 on real yields falling after the sweep. Silver is 52.536 and plus 0.54% - a quarter of gold's move - and still minus 14.35% on the month. Copper is 6.3621, minus 0.64% today and minus 3.33% on the week, with LME three-month around 13,883 dollars a tonne. The reason is now explicit rather than inferred: BNP Paribas's head of metals strategy said few participants at the London industry gathering believed AI was a significant driver of copper demand, and analysts point out fibre optics cut copper content inside data centres. That is the physical market dismantling the premise the RBA, the BoJ and the RBNZ all cited when they turned hawkish - not equity sentiment doing it. The honest counterweight is that Chinese physical is tight, with the Yangshan premium near 200 dollars a tonne and close to a decade high, while roughly 80% of global visible inventory is now stranded in the United States and Comex stocks are up 60% this year. Copper is a US inventory distortion as much as a demand collapse, which is why it is a low-conviction short rather than a conviction one. The score changes follow all of this. Canada comes down from plus one to zero: the energy shock Macklem named as the source of the inflation he is hiking against has deflated 15% in a week, and TradingEconomics now carries 2.50% for the December 9 decision, which is a hold rather than the hike this file leaned toward yesterday - so ratePaths.CAD flips with it. Switzerland comes down from plus two to plus one on one specific fact: the 1.5% October print that earned the upgrade was about 96% energy, and that energy is now falling, so the Q1/27 pass-through case is weaker than it looked twenty-four hours ago. Australia goes from zero to minus one, and the evidence is the crosses rather than a forecast: it lost against all seven other currencies today and is minus 0.31% on the week against a dollar that fell 0.77%, which is the only major to lose ground to a falling dollar. The euro stays at plus one despite the 4-handle, because the composition is the same energy that is rolling over, core has been stuck at 2.5% for months, monthly momentum eased to plus 0.4% from plus 0.6%, and negotiated wages are 2.44% - Nagel saying a December hike is very likely necessary is the hawkish counterweight and the reason it is not a downgrade. Sterling holds plus two into its own event, but GBP/USD comes off HIGH conviction to MEDIUM: at 93.5% priced the hike pays nothing, Reuters reports the Bank may use the Report to push back on bets for several more hikes, and the energy input that justified this hike is 15% lower than when the forecast round closed. The cleanest expressions today are the ones where a wide score gap sits on a weak leg with no scheduled repair: GBP/AUD, EUR/AUD and CAD/JPY. The cleanest thing to avoid is chasing crude lower.

today.headline: October flash HICP hit 4.0% from 3.8%, the first 4-handle in three years, and Nagel said a December hike is very likely necessary.
today.read: This is the day's biggest data fact and it is genuinely two-sided, which is why the score holds at plus one rather than rising. The hawkish half is real: 4.0% exactly matched the Reuters consensus, it is the first time the bloc has touched 4% since September 2023, Bundesbank President Nagel followed it by saying a December increase is very likely necessary, and that lands on a Governing Council Lagarde has already confirmed discussed hiking on October 29 before holding unanimously. Pricing reads above 72%. The dovish half is the composition, and it is now time-critical. Energy inflation jumped to 20.8% from 18.9% and did effectively all the work; core held at 2.5% where it has sat for months; monthly momentum eased to plus 0.4% from plus 0.6%; negotiated wages are 2.44%. The euro area's energy input is gas rather than crude, and gas is minus 13.01% on the week at 85.18 while still plus 12.54% on the month - so the rollover shows up in the November and December prints the ECB will actually have in hand on December 17, not in this one. The currency confirms the ambivalence: EUR/USD is 1.12620 and plus 0.30% today, plus 0.73% on the week but only plus 0.02% on the month, and the euro gained on every cross it should have - EUR/AUD plus 0.24%, EUR/GBP plus 0.15%, EUR/CAD plus 0.10% - while losing fractionally to the franc and the yen. Express it against the Australian dollar and the Canadian dollar rather than against the dollar. Eurostat finalises the October components on November 18.

today.headline: The Middle East energy shock Macklem named as the source of Canadian inflation fell 14.52% on the week, and TradingEconomics now forecasts a December hold.
today.read: This is the clearest thesis break on the board and it is a downgrade from plus one to zero. Two days ago Macklem told the Commons Standing Committee on Finance that further hikes may be needed, put CPI at 3.5% by year-end and at or above 3% through much of 2027, and attributed the pickup specifically to the Middle East energy shock rather than domestic demand. That was the firmest language he had used and this file upgraded on it. The input underneath it has now collapsed: WTI settled 8.3% lower on Wednesday, is 87.186 and minus 14.52% on the week, gasoline is minus 12.38% and heating oil minus 9.43%. TradingEconomics has moved with it and carries 2.50% for December 9, a hold on the 2.50% set October 28. The forward case is not dead - he explicitly said decisions are meeting by meeting, and he said he would update the Bank's forecast once today's federal budget lands - but the counterweights are now the heavier side: core at 2.2% is the softest here outside Switzerland and Japan, September employment was minus 68,300, and he named spare capacity himself. He also agreed that record federal borrowing leaves Ottawa exposed to bond-market trouble, which makes today's budget a two-sided event rather than a dovish one. USD/CAD is 1.39513 and minus 0.19% today, still minus 1.80% on the month from when crude was bid. Friday's employment print at plus 14.6k, the same minute as US payrolls, is the resolution. Express the downgrade through CAD/JPY and against the euro rather than against a dollar that has its own problem.

today.headline: The Bank of England hikes to 4.00% at 12:00Z on a 7-0-2 vote forecast, 93.5% priced, into energy that is 15% cheaper than when the forecast round closed.
today.read: Sterling stays at the top of this board, but the way to hold it changed this morning. The event is as dated and as priced as events get: TradingEconomics carries a 4.00% consensus and forecast from 3.75%, ForexFactory a 7-0-2 vote against September's 3-0-6 hold, the Reuters economist poll 7-2 with Taylor and Dhingra named the likely holds, Polymarket 93.5% against 6.5% for no change, and it would be the first hike since August 2023. MUFG expects 50bp in total starting today, which is the actual reason to own sterling - the second hike, not this one. What changed is the asymmetry. At 93.5% the hike pays almost nothing, Reuters reports the Bank may use the Monetary Policy Report to push back on bets for several more increases, and the energy that drove UK CPI to 3.5% with core at 2.8% is 12% to 15% cheaper than when the Bank's forecast round closed - UK gas alone is minus 12.50% on the week. A Report that keeps a 4-handle on the CPI profile extends this trade; one that caps the path at 4.00%, or a Bailey press conference at 12:30Z that leans on falling energy, takes sterling off the top of this board inside the hour. So GBP/USD comes off HIGH to MEDIUM while the wide relative trades stay on. The underlying data is still the best here and still domestic: unemployment fell to 4.7%, employment was plus 102,000 and wage growth is 3.7%. GBP/USD is 1.34916 and plus 1.63% on the month, the best of any major.

today.headline: Democrats swept both chambers and the dollar hit a one-month low, but ADP beat at plus 86,000 and December hike pricing rebuilt to roughly 76% to 82%.
today.read: The verdict and the forward disagree here, and that disagreement is the trade. Backward-looking, the dollar is weak: the sweep is confirmed rather than probable, the Dow jumped 1,569 points or about 3%, the ten-year fell 8.8 basis points to 4.886% and the two-year to 4.58%, and DXY is 101.250, minus 0.24% today, minus 0.77% on the week and at a one-month low. Every other currency here gained against it. But the channel was fiscal, not monetary - divided government read as removing deficit expansion and Treasury borrowing - and that story is now fully resolved and in the price. The rate case went the other way. October ADP private payrolls printed plus 86,000 against a forecast near 75,000, and December hike odds rebuilt to roughly 76% to 82% across trackers from the 71% to 73% carried yesterday, though those sources are secondary and conflict with each other, so treat the direction as the signal rather than the level. Underneath, this is the only hawkish case on this board that never rested on energy: CPI is 3.7%, core 2.6%, PPI 6.3%, and the Fed held October 28 by 10-2 with both dissents for a hike. So the forward is hawkish while the verdict is mixed, and FXStreet's framing of the election-inspired setback as a possible buying opportunity ahead of Friday is the honest read. Friday's payrolls at plus 65,000 with unemployment forecast unchanged at 4.2% and earnings at plus 0.3% resolves it. A beat rebuilds December and the dollar together; a miss with unemployment rising sends this to minus one and extends every long against it.

today.headline: The Australian dollar lost against all seven other currencies and is minus 0.31% on the week against a dollar that fell 0.77%, with both legs of the RBA hike now contested.
today.read: Downgraded from zero to minus one, and the evidence is the cross board rather than a forecast. AUD/USD is 0.70079 and managed plus 0.04% on a day the dollar fell 0.24%; on the week it is minus 0.31% while DXY is minus 0.77%, which makes it the only major to lose ground to a falling dollar. It lost on every single cross today: EUR/AUD plus 0.24%, GBP/AUD plus 0.10%, AUD/JPY minus 0.27%, AUD/CHF minus 0.29%, AUD/NZD minus 0.35%, AUD/CAD minus 0.15%. Both legs the November 3 hike was built on are now under attack at once. The statement cited elevated fuel and commodity prices - fuel is minus 14.52% on the week. It cited AI-related demand for technology goods, and the November Statement on Monetary Policy repeats that AI-related demand has helped trading-partner growth - but BNP Paribas's head of metals strategy has now said few participants at the London industry gathering believed AI was a significant driver of copper demand, with analysts noting fibre optics cut copper content inside data centres. Copper is 6.3621 and minus 3.33% on the week with LME three-month near 13,883 dollars, below September's 14,875 record. What holds this at minus one rather than lower is the 4.85% cash rate, the highest on this board and the highest in Australia since 2008, plus a tight Chinese physical copper market with the Yangshan premium near a decade high. Bullock gave no guidance, December 8 reads as a hold, and the minutes on November 17 are the next read on the three dissenters. A copper recovery repairs this quickly and is the thing to watch rather than the domestic data.

today.headline: The franc held its gains on most crosses, but the energy that was 96% of its CPI surprise has now fallen 12% to 15%, so the score comes back to plus one.
today.read: Downgraded from plus two to plus one on one specific fact rather than on price action. Yesterday's upgrade rested on the October CPI surprise - 1.5% year over year against a 1.3% consensus and 1.0% in September, the highest since 2023 - and on the argument that the energy pass-through was unfinished, which made the TradingEconomics 0.25% for Q1/27 credible. The composition was honest at the time: energy was roughly 96% of the net monthly increase, CPI excluding petroleum products was unchanged and core held at 0.5%. What changed in twenty-four hours is that the energy input collapsed. Brent is minus 15.07% on the week and heating oil minus 9.43%, so the pass-through that was supposed to keep pushing Swiss headline inflation higher into the fourth quarter is now pushing the other way, and the Q1/27 date is less credible than it looked, not more. The haven leg is unaffected and is why this stays positive rather than neutral: the franc gained again on most crosses today with USD/CHF 0.81436 and minus 0.34%, minus 1.22% on the week and minus 2.08% on the month, EUR/CHF 0.91716 and minus 0.05%, GBP/CHF minus 0.19%, AUD/CHF minus 0.29%, CAD/CHF minus 0.14%, and it worked through both the Nasdaq correction and the gold liquidation when the yen did not. Hormuz diplomacy going backwards - Iran rejecting Washington's response on November 4 - keeps that bid intact. Policy is still the ceiling at 0.00% with December 10 a hold inside the 0% to 2% band, though FXStreet reported in late October that Swiss policymakers have scaled back their direct intervention threats, which removes one cap.

today.headline: Hawkish minutes kept December 18 alive and the yen gained for a second day, but again only against the dollar.
today.read: Held at plus one with the same qualification that has applied all week, and it is the reason not to size this against anything other than the dollar. Minutes released overnight read hawkish and reaffirmed December bets; the Bank has indicated underlying inflation has reached its 2% target, Takata dissented at the October 30 meeting for an immediate move to 1.5%, FY2027 inflation was lifted to 2.6% from 2.4%, swaps imply 75% to 80% and TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50%, with one wire calling December nearly fully priced. But USD/JPY at 157.893 and minus 0.35% was a dollar move once more: EUR/JPY was minus 0.03%, CHF/JPY minus 0.01%, NZD/JPY plus 0.03%, and only AUD/JPY at minus 0.27% and GBP/JPY at minus 0.19% showed real yen gains. On the week USD/JPY is actually plus 0.11%. Two things cap this. Katayama issued a fresh intervention warning that the wires describe as failing to impress yen bulls, and the reason the pair sits near 158 is that warning rather than demand for yen - Japan and the United States spent a record 15.4 trillion yen between July 30 and August 26 defending it. The 200-day average at 158.65 is the level that matters, with 160.00 to 160.50 above. And the hawkish case has the same soft leg as Australia's: Ueda named strong global AI demand as a price pressure, and the copper market has now said out loud that it does not believe AI drives its demand. Express the yen against the Australian and Canadian dollars, not against the dollar, and respect Ueda at 16:00Z Friday.

today.headline: Quiet on data, up 0.32% against the dollar and better than the Aussie for once, with Saturday's election now a genuine coin flip.
today.read: Held at minus two and still the board's short leg, but today was a mild reprieve rather than more damage. NZD/USD is 0.56408 and plus 0.32%, roughly in line with a dollar that fell 0.24%, and for the first time this week the kiwi beat the Australian dollar with AUD/NZD minus 0.35% - the largest move on any AUD cross. It also gained fractionally on sterling and the euro, with GBP/NZD minus 0.11% and EUR/NZD minus 0.03%. The damage is still the data and it has not changed: Q3 unemployment at 5.7% is the highest since 2016, private wages slowed to 2.0% against 3.7% inflation, employment fell 0.1% on the quarter with Q2 revised down to plus 0.3%, and participation fell to 70.4%. December 9 remains a genuine split - TradingEconomics and UOB carry 3.00%, Westpac still forecasts a hike and the October hold was 4-3 with members agreeing further tightening would likely be needed, while Moody's argues weak wages and falling real incomes back another hold. One leg of the hawkish case weakened today without any New Zealand news at all: the RBNZ built its 4.4% December inflation forecast on fuel pass-through, and fuel is minus 14.52% on the week. Saturday's election is now a true binary rather than background. The final 1News-Verian poll has National 30% and Labour 29%, the National-led bloc projected at 58 seats and short of a majority without Opportunity's seven, and Opportunity sitting on the 5% threshold as kingmaker. Labour has pledged to restore the RBNZ's dual employment mandate; Westpac notes December 9 proceeds under the current single mandate regardless, so this is a February-and-beyond institutional risk, but it is live now rather than hypothetical. Keep kiwi shorts on the crosses small into the weekend.

geopolitics: The Strait of Hormuz is still closed and the oil premium has come out anyway, and the gap between those two facts is the most tradeable thing on this board. Brent settled 8.98 dollars or 8.7% lower at 94.62 on Wednesday and WTI fell 7.97 dollars or 8.3% to 88.12 - the largest single-session break since the closure began. TradingEconomics now has Brent at 94.106 and minus 15.07% on the week, WTI at 87.186 and minus 14.52%, gasoline minus 12.38% and heating oil minus 9.43%, with the gas complex following at last: EU gas 85.18 and minus 13.01% on the week, German gas 89.58 and minus 12.17%, UK gas minus 12.50%. Three things drove it, and only one of them is about the Strait. Trump said there are no immediate plans to strike Iran; the Democratic sweep of both chambers was read as constraining his military options, with Vance urging an agreement after the loss and Qatar pushing a draft that could restart direct talks within days; and, the substantive one, Middle Eastern oil exports have recovered to roughly pre-war levels, so the market has concluded the barrels are getting out regardless. What did not happen is a reopening or even progress toward one. Iran rejected Washington's response to its conditions for reopening Hormuz on November 4, Tehran has sharply increased attacks on shipping in the Strait, and only seven commodity vessels transited on Thursday against seventeen a day earlier - which is the counter to Treasury Secretary Bessent describing vessel movement as increasing day by day. So crude is now priced for a resolution Iran has formally refused, and the risk from 87 dollars is asymmetric to the upside. That is why USOIL is a RANGE rather than a short after a 15% week, and why the Canadian dollar sits at zero rather than negative. The FX transmission runs the other way from the way it has run all autumn, and it runs through six of these eight currencies at once. The Bank of England hikes to 4.00% today because energy pushed UK CPI to 3.5%. The euro area printed a 4.0% October HICP on energy at 20.8%, against core stuck at 2.5%. Switzerland's 1.5% CPI surprise was roughly 96% energy. Macklem told the Commons finance committee on November 3 that Canadian inflation came from the Middle East energy shock rather than domestic demand, and TradingEconomics has since flipped December 9 to a hold. The RBA built its November 3 hike on elevated fuel. The RBNZ's 4.4% December inflation forecast rests on fuel pass-through. Every one of those is a hawkish case measured on prices that have fallen 12% to 15% in five sessions - so the hikes still land, and it is the paths beyond them that are now mispriced to the dovish side. The two exceptions are the trades. The United States never needed the energy premium: CPI 3.7%, core 2.6%, PPI 6.3%, two October dissents for a hike, and December pricing rebuilt to roughly 76% to 82% on an ADP beat. And the franc keeps its haven bid precisely because the diplomacy failed, even as the inflation half of its case weakens.
